# Towards a classification of stem cells

## Authors

- Lucie Laplane<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0003-0185-3323](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0185-3323)) †
- Eric Solary<sup>2</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-8629-1341](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-8629-1341))

### Affiliations

1. Institut d’Histoire et Philosophie des Sciences et des Techniques Université Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne Paris France
2. Département d’Hématologie Institut de Cancérologie Gustave Roussy Villejuif France
3. Faculté de Médecine Université Paris-Sud Le Kremlin-Bicêtre France

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

The characteristic properties of stem cells – notably their ability to self-renew and to differentiate – have meant that they have traditionally been viewed as distinct from most other types of cells. However, recent research has blurred the line between stem cells and other cells by showing that the former display a range of behaviors in different tissues and at different stages of development. Here, we use the tools of metaphysics to describe a classification scheme for stem cells, and to highlight what their inherent diversity means for cancer treatment.

## One size does not fit all

Stem cells have been described as a discrete population of cells sitting at the apex of a hierarchy of irreversible cell differentiation. This view has had an impact on the way in which stem cell research is performed by, for example, encouraging the idea that specific markers may help to distinguish and sort stem cells. However, researchers discovered that certain tissues showed much more plasticity in cell fate than anticipated. For example, it appeared that intestinal cells could replace the stem cells tasked with renewing the lining of the bowel (Tetteh et al., 2016). Such flexibility suggested that stemness might not be restricted to a pre-defined population of cells and prompted some biologists to question what stem cells really were.

Traditional views of stem cells arose from studies of the hematopoietic tissue in the bone marrow, where blood cells originate in adults. However, in the late 1970s, Ray Schofield suggested that stemness actually relies on the interaction of hematopoietic stem cells (the cells that give rise to other blood cells) with the microenvironment in which they reside (Schofield, 1978). Although long denied, the importance of this 'niche' is now increasingly accepted: hematopoietic stem cells cannot be understood out of their context, which may account for the difficulties in maintaining them in culture.

Finally, new technologies, such as lineage tracing, have further questioned the boundaries of the stem cell category, as studies have shown that not every individual hematopoietic stem cell appears to be multipotent (discussed in Haas et al., 2018). These analyses highlighted that non-hematopoietic stem cells, called multipotent progenitors, could unexpectedly maintain the production of hematopoietic cells over an extended period of time (Sun et al., 2014). These are only a few of the examples that illustrate the potential diversity of these cells, which has resulted in two opposite views of what a stem cell is: it can either be an entity, a discrete population of cells with stable properties, or it can be a cell state, a property that is acquired in a specific context (e.g. Clevers and Watt, 2018; Zipori, 2004).

## Some order in the stemness mess

Philosophy, and more specifically metaphysics, has a long tradition of characterizing and distinguishing different types of properties for the objects or systems around us. We recently used this tradition to characterize stemness and our analysis led us to the conclusion that four types of properties may exist under the guise of stemness (Laplane, 2016; Laplane and Solary, 2017).

Stemness can be a 'categorical' property, that is, an intrinsic feature that is independent of any interaction with surrounding entities, such as the atomic mass of an element. It was initially assumed that all stem cells belong to this class, but, as discussed below, it might only apply to certain cancers.

Alternatively, stemness can be a 'dispositional' property, which is also an intrinsic feature, but one that only manifests upon interaction with external stimuli. For example, a fragile item only breaks on impact. Current knowledge suggests that healthy hematopoietic stem cells fall under this category. Although stemness is hardwired in these cells, it tightly depends on the bone marrow niche. In a malignant context, however, hematopoietic progenitor cells can gain stemness as they transform into malignant cells, questioning the maintenance of stemness as a dispositional property.

Stemness can also be a 'relational' property that relies on the interaction between entities. For example, body weight depends on gravity, and differs on the Earth and the Moon. Unlike the dispositional property, a relational property is not hardwired in a predetermined pool of cells, such as germline stem cells (which give rise to egg and sperm cells). When these stem cells are removed in fruit flies and mice, they are replaced by differentiated cells that migrate back to the stem cell niche, where they reacquire stemness (e.g. Brawley and Matunis, 2004). Stemness could also be a relational property in some cancers: recent research in a mouse model of colon cancer has revealed that after cancer stem cells had been eliminated, some remaining cancer cells regained stemness in the primary tumor but not in liver metastases, suggesting that a specific niche is required for the acquisition of stemness (de Sousa e Melo et al., 2017).

Finally, stemness can be a 'systemic' property, defined as an extrinsic characteristic that is provided and maintained by the system. For example, in the Matrix movie, every time the main antagonist Agent Smith is killed, the system transforms any human to incarnate the agent. Likewise, stemness is a systemic property when non-stem cells acquire stemness features in the absence of a specific environment, which may be the case in cancer. For example, some differentiated cells from breast cancer cell lines can become cancer stem cells again when cultured in vitro (Gupta et al., 2011). This suggests that stemness can be reacquired without a specific niche, with regulation taking place at the system level – here, the cancer cell population.

Stemness therefore encompasses distinct properties, depending on the tissue and context. Which category a stem cell population belongs to depends on two questions that can be addressed experimentally: first, can stemness be acquired by non-stem cells of that tissue? And second, is the niche mandatory for the acquisition of stemness, the expression of stemness, or both?

## Stemness in cancer

In oncology, the cancer stem cell model presupposes that cancers maintain an organization similar to that of healthy tissues, with a pool of malignant stem cells acting as the main reservoir for the production of every other cell of the tumor. These cells may be generated by the transformation of typical stem cells in the tissue of origin. The relationship between the rate of stem cell division and the risk of malignant transformation in a given tissue has led to much controversy in recent years (Tomasetti et al., 2017; Tomasetti and Vogelstein, 2015). Alternatively, cancer stem cells may emerge from non-stem cells endowed with stemness abilities thanks to genetic and epigenetic alterations. Similarities and dissimilarities between normal stem cells and cancer stem cells open three questions.

Firstly, is stemness the same in cancers and their non-pathological counterparts? Some data suggest that transformation can lead to, or rely on, a transition between two types of stemness. For instance, in some blood cancers known as myeloproliferative neoplasms, hematopoietic cells harboring the JAK2 V617F mutation (which can be found in the majority of patients) secrete a molecule that damages the hematopoietic niche (Arranz et al., 2014). Only healthy, but not malignant stem cells, are affected by the degradation of their environment, which suggests that upon transformation into leukemic stem cells, normal stem cells become independent to the niche. This moves stemness from a dispositional property in healthy hematopoietic stem cells to a categorical property in leukemic stem cells.

Secondly, does stemness remain the same type of property throughout disease progression? The JAK2 V617F mutation also contributes to shifting stemness from a dispositional to a categorical property by disrupting the regulation of hematopoietic stem cells by their environment (e.g., Staerk and Constantinescu, 2012). In other myeloid malignancies, oncogenic events such as KRAS mutations can lead to similar dysregulations. These mutations can occur either very early in leukemic transformation, or later during disease progression (Deininger et al., 2017). This suggests that stemness transitioning from a dispositional to a categorical property could also happen during the clonal evolution of the disease.

Lastly, is stemness the same type of property in all types of cancers of a particular tissue? In mouse models of squamous cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer, cells gain migratory and invasive properties through a mechanism known as a epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. This process can occur either frequently or rarely, depending on the chromatin state of the cell of origin (Latil et al., 2017). As this transition can result in stemness acquisition, squamous cell carcinomas may fall into two categories. In the absence of transition, stemness would best described as a dispositional property: intrinsic to the cells, but only revealed in the right context. However, in the presence of frequent transitions, stemness would become a relational property – extrinsic and conditional on epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions.

Taken together, cancer occurrence and progression could be associated with changes in the nature of stemness. It remains to be seen whether these changes are a consequence of disease progression or one of its requirements.

## How stemness categorization may drive therapeutic choices

How is this philosophical characterization of stemness useful for science and medicine? We suggest that in oncology, the four types of stemness properties require different therapeutic strategies. Current treatment approaches target either malignant cells (with chemotherapy, ionizing radiations and targeted therapies), or surrounding cells (with immunotherapy or anti-angiogenic therapies). If these treatments fail to eliminate all the cancer stem cells, a relapse may occur. Choosing to target either cancer stem cells, their niche, or both, relies on implicit presuppositions regarding stemness.

Targeting cancer stem cells depends on the assumption that stemness is an intrinsic property (i.e., categorical or dispositional); otherwise, the malignant cells would regenerate new cancer stem cells after their elimination. Niche-targeting relies on the notion that stemness is a niche-dependent property (i.e., dispositional or relational). Accordingly, each type of stemness may determine the choice of a therapeutic approach:

Changes in the nature of stemness may require therapeutic adaptation. It would thus be useful to monitor the impact of genetic and epigenetic alterations on the nature of stemness during the evolution of the disease. If changes in stemness are driving progression rather than resulting from it, therapeutic interventions that modulate stemness could also be beneficial.

## Perspective: is philosophy useful to science?

Stem cell biology is full of conceptual debates, and philosophers have contributed to these debates on a range of topics (reviewed in Fagan, 2013b), including the definition of stem cells and the entity/state debate (Fagan, 2013a; Laplane, 2016; Wilson et al., 2007; Leychkis et al., 2009). Focusing on the nature of stemness, we show how traditional tools of philosophy, such as the metaphysics of properties, can be applied to stem cell biology to shed light on the fundamental nature of stem cells. More than a simple descriptive characterization, the proposed classification draws practical consequences in guiding the choice of an anticancer treatment. Many questions remain unsolved, however. If stemness is not one but four different properties, are we right to use only one name? Are all the cells that we call stem cells, really stem cells? Do they share some underlying characteristics that justify their biological clustering, or is 'stem cell' just a convenient category to group cell types that are actually distinct?

While experimental biology will hardly answer these questions, phylogeny, on the other hand, could be helpful. For instance, mammals and insects have distinct types of eyes that have emerged independently throughout evolution as two different but effective solutions to a similar challenge. Similarly, a phylogenetic analysis of stemness could highlight whether the different types of stem cells occurred separately during evolution, as different solutions to the challenges of tissue maintenance and repair. In turn, this would deepen the metaphysics of stem cells by identifying whether our four stemness properties depict entities that are biologically independent . It is only by bridging disciplines such as experimental biology, medicine, phylogeny and philosophy that stem cells will be properly understood.

results.result: The authors propose a four-category classification of stemness based on metaphysical analysis of properties: categorical (intrinsic, context-independent), dispositional (intrinsic, context-dependent), relational (extrinsic, niche-dependent), and systemic (extrinsic, system-level). This classification depends on whether stemness can be acquired by non-stem cells and whether the niche is mandatory for acquisition or expression of stemness.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C36 establish a coherent philosophical framework for classifying stemness. The definitions are logically consistent and grounded in metaphysical tradition (C18, C21, C25, C31). The classification criteria (C36) provide testable experimental questions. The framework is supported by the authors' prior published work (C17) and represents a systematic application of philosophical tools to biological phenomena.

results.result: Healthy hematopoietic stem cells exhibit stemness as a dispositional property that is hardwired but tightly depends on the bone marrow niche. This niche-dependence may explain difficulties in maintaining these cells in culture.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 are supported by established knowledge about hematopoietic stem cells and their niche dependence (C9, C11, C12). The classification as dispositional property is consistent with the observation that stemness is intrinsic but requires environmental interaction. However, C13 remains speculative about culture difficulties, though it is a reasonable inference from niche dependence.

results.result: Germline stem cells in fruit flies and mice demonstrate relational stemness: when removed, differentiated cells migrate to the niche and reacquire stemness, showing that this property is not hardwired in a predetermined pool.
results.evaluation: Claim C28 is supported by citation to Brawley and Matunis, 2004, providing experimental evidence for plasticity in germline stem cell identity. This observation directly supports the relational property classification (C26), as stemness is acquired through niche interaction rather than being predetermined. The example effectively demonstrates the distinction from dispositional properties.

results.result: In a mouse model of colon cancer, remaining cancer cells regained stemness in the primary tumor but not in liver metastases after cancer stem cell elimination, suggesting niche-specific requirements for stemness acquisition.
results.evaluation: Claim C29 is supported by citation to de Sousa e Melo et al., 2017, providing experimental evidence. The differential regaining of stemness between primary and metastatic sites (C30) logically supports the inference that a specific niche is required. This provides strong evidence for relational stemness in some cancers.

results.result: Differentiated cells from breast cancer cell lines can reacquire cancer stem cell properties in vitro without a specific niche, suggesting stemness as a systemic property regulated at the population level.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 is supported by citation to Gupta et al., 2011. The inference (C34) that stemness can be reacquired without a specific niche is reasonable given the in vitro context. This provides evidence for systemic property classification (C32), though the mechanism of system-level regulation remains incompletely characterized.

results.result: In myeloproliferative neoplasms, the JAK2 V617F mutation causes niche damage that affects healthy but not malignant stem cells, indicating transformation shifts stemness from a dispositional to a categorical property through niche independence.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 are supported by citation to Arranz et al., 2014, providing experimental evidence. The inference that malignant stem cells become niche-independent (C44) is reasonable from the differential sensitivity. The classification shift from dispositional to categorical (C45-C46) logically follows from the change in niche dependence, supported by citation to Staerk and Constantinescu, 2012.

results.result: KRAS mutations in myeloid malignancies can cause similar dysregulations to JAK2 V617F and may occur early or late in disease progression, suggesting stemness transitions could happen during clonal evolution.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 is supported by citation to Deininger et al., 2017. However, C47 lacks specific citation for the similarity claim, and C49 is explicitly speculative. The inference that stemness transitions occur during clonal evolution is logical but requires direct experimental validation of property changes at different disease stages.

results.result: In squamous cell carcinoma, the frequency of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (which depends on chromatin state) determines whether stemness is dispositional (rare transitions) or relational (frequent transitions).
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by experimental data from mouse models (C51 cites Latil et al., 2017). The relationship between EMT and stemness acquisition (C52) is presented as established knowledge. The inferences about property classification (C53-C54) logically follow from the frequency of transitions and are consistent with the proposed framework, though direct experimental validation of the property type would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Cancer occurrence and progression could be associated with changes in the nature of stemness, though whether these changes are causal or consequential remains unresolved.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 is a speculative synthesis of the presented examples. Claim C56 explicitly acknowledges the unresolved causal relationship. While the examples provide suggestive evidence for stemness changes during cancer progression, the directionality and mechanistic relationship require further experimental investigation. This represents an important open question rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: Different types of stemness properties require distinct therapeutic strategies: targeting cancer stem cells assumes intrinsic stemness, while niche-targeting assumes niche-dependent stemness. Changes in stemness during disease may require therapeutic adaptation and monitoring.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 present logically sound inferences about the presuppositions underlying different therapeutic approaches. The logical framework is internally consistent: if stemness is not intrinsic, targeting stem cells alone would be insufficient (C60). Claims C62-C64 are speculative recommendations but follow logically from the classification framework. The therapeutic implications are conceptually sound though require prospective clinical validation.

results.result: Recent research has revealed unexpected plasticity in stem cell behavior: intestinal cells can replace bowel stem cells, not all hematopoietic stem cells are multipotent, and multipotent progenitors can maintain hematopoiesis long-term. This diversity has led to two opposing views of stem cells as either entities or states.
results.evaluation: Claims are supported by appropriate citations (C5: Tetteh et al., 2016; C14: Haas et al., 2018; C15: Sun et al., 2014; C16: Clevers and Watt, 2018; Zipori, 2004). These observations collectively challenge traditional views and provide empirical motivation for the classification framework. The evidence demonstrates genuine biological diversity in stem cell behavior across tissues.

results.result: Philosophical tools, particularly the metaphysics of properties, can be applied to stem cell biology to clarify fundamental concepts and guide practical decisions such as cancer treatment selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 establish that philosophers have contributed to stem cell debates, supported by multiple citations. Claims C67-C68 assert the utility of the philosophical approach demonstrated in this manuscript. The paper successfully demonstrates how metaphysical analysis can organize biological observations into a coherent framework with therapeutic implications, supporting the claim of practical utility.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis could determine whether different stemness types evolved independently and whether they represent biologically independent entities, requiring interdisciplinary collaboration for complete understanding.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 are explicitly speculative proposals for future research. While the phylogenetic approach is conceptually interesting and could provide valuable insights, no such analysis is presented. The claim about interdisciplinary necessity (C72) is normative rather than empirical. These represent promising research directions rather than established results.

results.result: Traditional views characterized stem cells as discrete populations with self-renewal and differentiation abilities, sitting at the apex of irreversible differentiation hierarchies. This view arose from hematopoietic studies and influenced research approaches including marker-based identification.
results.evaluation: These claims describe established historical knowledge about stem cell biology and the development of the field. They accurately represent the traditional conceptual framework that the manuscript challenges. The claims are presented as background knowledge and are consistent with the history of stem cell research.

results.result: The cancer stem cell model posits that cancers maintain hierarchical organization with malignant stem cells as the main reservoir. Cancer stem cells may arise from transformed normal stem cells or from non-stem cells acquiring stemness. Treatment failure to eliminate all cancer stem cells may lead to relapse.
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C57-C58 describe established concepts in cancer biology. Claims C38 and C40 present alternative hypotheses for cancer stem cell origin, appropriately marked as speculative. Claim C39 is supported by citations to Tomasetti et al. These claims provide necessary background for understanding the therapeutic implications of the stemness classification.

results.result: It was initially assumed all stem cells have categorical stemness, but this may only apply to certain cancers. Hematopoietic progenitor cells can gain stemness during malignant transformation, questioning the dispositional property model.
results.evaluation: Claim C19 describes a historical assumption. Claim C20 is explicitly speculative about categorical stemness in cancers. Claim C24 presents an observation that challenges the dispositional model but lacks specific citation. While these claims contribute to the conceptual framework, the evidence for categorical stemness being restricted to certain cancers requires more direct experimental support.
